name: Sprintz
baseline: FastPFOR, SIMD-BP128 and Simple8B (the integer compressors the repo README says were run against Sprintz), plus general-purpose byte compressors
workload: Lossless compression of multivariate integer time series (8-bit and 16-bit quantized AMPDs, MSRC-12, PAMAP, UCI Gas and UCR datasets), measuring compression ratio and decompression speed.
claimed_speedup: README: 'state-of-the-art compression ratios, and can decompress at multiple GB/s in a single thread'. Paper abstract (seen only as a search-result snippet, arXiv was blocked): 'decompress at over 3GB/s in a single thread, even faster than many algorithms with much lower compression ratios'. No per-baseline speed ratio against FastPFOR or Simple8B was read.
compiler_and_flags: README says 'only tested with Clang on OS X'; flags not stated
tradeoffs: Targets small-memory streaming blocks of integer time series (forecasting plus bit packing), so it is not a drop-in for sorted posting lists. Integer baselines were run on data zero-padded to 32 bits, as the README states. Benchmark driver lives in a separate lzbench fork and Python harness.
caveats: Headline speed number comes from the paper abstract snippet only; the paper PDF and the results/ directory numbers were not readable here. The README does not state CPU model or compiler flags, and only Clang on OS X is said to be tested. The main claim is compression ratio; speed is claimed relative to 'many algorithms', not to FastPFOR specifically. Last commit is more than 5 years old.
found_via: GitHub topics page for integer compression plus search for Sprintz paper; README opened at github.com/dblalock/sprintz

name: LeCo (Learn-to-Compress)
baseline: Frame-of-Reference (FOR), Delta encoding and Elias-Fano (microbenchmarks); Parquet/Arrow and RocksDB default configurations (system tests)
workload: Lightweight compression of integer columns (fixed-length FOR/Delta/LeCo and variable-length Delta/LeCo variants) measured by compression ratio and random access speed, then integrated into Arrow/Parquet and RocksDB index blocks.
claimed_speedup: From search-result snippets of the SIGMOD'24 paper (paper PDF blocked, snippet only): 'Pareto improvement on both compression ratio and random access speed over existing algorithms'; up to 5x faster multi-column filter-groupby-aggregation query; bitmap aggregation up to 11.8x with 60.5% memory reduction; 16% better RocksDB throughput than its default configuration. The repo README itself gives no numbers.
hardware: README requires Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS; CPU model not stated on the page
tradeoffs: Learned (regression-based) model per segment instead of a fixed frame, so it adds model parameters and training/partitioning cost at encode time. Targets immutable columnar data with random access, not streaming SIMD bit packing.
caveats: No LICENSE file found at the repo root (LICENSE, LICENSE.md and LICENSE.txt returned 404), so code must not be copied. All numbers come from search snippets, not an opened paper page, and the snippet does not say which baseline each system-level number is against. Baselines (FOR, Delta, Elias-Fano) are not the named incumbents of this category; FastPFOR and Simple8b are not confirmed as benchmarked.
found_via: WebSearch for the LeCo paper code; repo README and commits page opened on github.com

name: Apache ORC C++ AVX-512 RLE bit-unpacking (ORC-1356)
baseline: ORC C++ scalar RLE bit-packing decoder (pre-change)
workload: Decoding of RLE v2 bit-packed integer runs with widths 1 to 32 bits, comparing AVX-512 decode against the scalar decoder.
claimed_speedup: PR author: 'average 6X ~ 7X performance latency improvement' for AVX-512 over the baseline scalar decoder.
compiler_and_flags: CMake option BUILD_ENABLE_AVX512 (default OFF); optimization flags not stated on the PR page; runtime override via ORC_USER_SIMD_LEVEL
hardware: Intel AVX-512 (Skylake-X class) processor; exact CPU model not stated on the page
tradeoffs: AVX-512 path is opt-in at build time and selected at run time; scalar path remains. The commits page also shows a later RVV (RISC-V vector) bit-unpacking change (ORC-2216) for the same decoder.
caveats: First-party PR claim with a micro-benchmark and no stated CPU model or flags. PR comments report minimal or no improvement when integrated into ClickHouse, so the gain is data-dependent. Baseline is ORC's own scalar decoder, not varint, Simple8b or FastPFor. The PR was merged on 2023-05-07.
found_via: WebSearch for AVX-512 bitpacking C++ README benchmark; PR opened at github.com/apache/orc/pull/1375
